body.p: Claims 1, 6-9, and 12-13 have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Kahn (US 2018/0143642) in view of Brinklow.
Claims 2-4 and 10-11 have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Kahn in view of Brinklow, and further in view of Gao (US 2018/0201227).
Claim 5 has been rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Kahn, Brinklow and Gao, and further in view of Visintainer (US 2021/0118295)
Independent claims 1 and 9 have been amended to more clearly recite that which the applicant regards as patentable.
In the claims, an automatic determination of threatening behavior is made by detection of a specific threat situation from sensor information. The threat situation involves two co-joined actions.
The automatic determined is made by interpretation of sensor information with a controller.
Also, in the claims, evasive action is automatically controlled.
These aspects of the claims are not taught or reasonably suggested by the proposed combinations of references.

Kahn only discloses human detection of a threatening situation and human activation of an emergency escape mode (EEM). Referring to block 450 of figure 4, which Kahn states is for an autonomous vehicle, Kahn teaches: "an emergency escape mode is triggered by a user. The user may trigger the emergency escape mode by a button press, voice command, gesture, a combination of those, or other suitable mechanism" (paragraph 41).
There is no analysis of surroundings for threats by a controller in Kahn even though surroundings may be assessed to determine an evasive action or perform autonomous driving actions.

The Office Action acknowledges that Kahn fails to disclose detecting that a first surrounding vehicle directly in front of the vehicle slows down in the absence of a traffic related reason to slow down.
The Office Action attempts to cure this teaching deficiency of Kahn with

teachings from Brinklow. But Brinklow is a news article describing a specific incident involving a cab driver that attacked a vehicle. This article might be representative of the dangers of road rage, but there is nothing in Brinklow that teaches or reasonably suggests making the claimed determination from sensor information by interpreting that information or automatically controlling an evasive maneuver.
It also cannot be determined what technological aspects the person of ordinary skill in the art might take from Brinklow to modify Kahn.

Never the less, even if Kahn and Brinklow are somehow combined, that which is claimed would not result. Missing from the combination would be all of that which is claimed as represented by the following quotation of claim 1:
automatically determining that one or more surrounding vehicles
demonstrates threatening behavior by:
- acquiring, with one or more sensors mounted on the vehicle, information regarding a first surrounding vehicle directly in front of the vehicle; and

- interpreting the information, with a controller, to detect that the first surrounding vehicle slows down in an absence of a traffic related reason to slow down in conjunction with detecting, based on further information from the one or more sensors, that a person approaches the vehicle; and upon determining that the one or more surrounding vehicles demonstrates threatening behavior, the controller automatically controlling the vehicle to perform one or more threat evasive actions.
The other references, even if added to the combination, still fail to address that which is claimed. For instance, while Gao might alert a user to a potential threat and
Visintainer monitors for potential collisions, adding the teachings of these references to the combination fail to cure the deficiencies of the Kahn/Brinklow combination.
For at least these reasons, a prima facie case of obviousness is lacking and withdrawal of the rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 103 is respectfully requested.
